title: Outflow rate limits are deliberately looser than inflow limits, often unlimited, to prioritize fast exits
content:
A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.1.3 defines inflows as "movements that raise exposure or capital allocated to an Instance or market, such as depositing, minting, or rebalancing into a position," and A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.1.4 defines outflows as "withdrawals, redemptions, or unwind operations" that lower exposure. The two directions are rate-limited separately, and the asymmetry is explicit: "Outflow limits are often configured **more permissively to prioritize safety and fast exits**. When outflow limits are 'unlimited,' the rate limits contract simply does not apply a cap in that direction."

The reasoning is that the two directions carry opposite risk. A rapid inflow is how an attacker or a mistake creates exposure; a rapid outflow is how the system removes it. Throttling both symmetrically would mean the same mechanism that contains an attack also delays the response to it — an Agent trying to unwind a deteriorating position, or Sky trying to pull capital from a failing venue, would be rate-limited by its own defence.

So the design accepts a one-directional guarantee: getting into a position is bounded, getting out is not. That is the right default for a stablecoin balance sheet, where the tail risk being managed is illiquidity rather than sudden deleveraging.

It also composes with the Asset Liability Management restrictions in the Allocation System definition (A.2.2.10.1). ALM constrains deployment into assets that cannot be exited quickly; unlimited outflow limits ensure the protocol's own machinery does not add friction to exits ALM has already made possible.
description: Inflows raise exposure and are throttled; outflows reduce it and are configured permissively, so the containment mechanism never becomes an obstacle to unwinding a position.
